paras: The mob attack on Sheriff J. H. Hutchinson took place at Washington, Washington County, Texas, on January 24, 1882, when a crowd turned on the county sheriff after a constable held for murder escaped from his custody. The crowd cursed and assaulted him, and by one account brought a rope and nearly hanged him before cooler heads intervened. Hutchinson survived and was later indicted for negligently permitting the escape.

On a Saturday night in January 1882, Alfred D. Gee, a constable at Washington, was reported to have shot Dr. Moeller, a young dentist, who died early the next morning. Gee was arrested the next day and held under guard until Tuesday, when he was turned over to Sheriff Hutchinson of Brenham, the county seat, for a preliminary examination set for one o'clock. According to the Brenham Banner's informant, the sheriff let Gee walk about town alone and left him with his attorneys in a vacant room over Dr. F. H. Smith's drug store.

Between one and half past one, Gee came down the inside stairway, went out the back door, mounted a horse hitched nearby and rode away, which at first drew no alarm because he had been allowed to move freely. When he failed to return after fifteen or twenty minutes, the people concluded that he had escaped.

The Banner reported that a crowd of between 125 and 150 men openly charged Hutchinson with turning Gee loose, called him "vile names" and "personally assaulted" him. In its version, the sheriff mounted a freedman's horse, ostensibly to pursue Gee, and was next heard of taking a train south to Hempstead; part of the crowd that had set out after Gee turned back to capture the sheriff but could not find him.

Henry Moeller, the dead man's brother, gave the Austin Statesman a harsher account: a crowd of several hundred took the sheriff "violently out into the street," brought a rope, and would have hanged him but for "a few cooler heads." He also said that Dr. Smith, who he said had furnished Gee a pistol, narrowly escaped lynching, whereas the Banner reported only that an unnamed citizen had been seen giving Gee a pistol.

According to the Statesman, the county attorney issued a warrant and had Hutchinson arrested, with an examination set for the following Monday. A petition for his removal was circulating at Washington, and Moeller said he would prosecute the sheriff for willfully allowing the escape. No arrest of anyone in the crowd was reported.

The county commissioners declared Gee's constable office vacant because he had broken custody and fled. In April the grand jury indicted Hutchinson for negligently permitting Gee, a prisoner charged with felony, to escape. By June Gee was again in custody, and Hutchinson took him to the Galveston jail for safe keeping to quiet fears of another escape.

Coverage found was limited to Texas papers apart from a one-line Brenham wire brief on the killing in the Wheeling Register. The Brenham Weekly Banner, published at the county seat, headlined its account "Culpable negligence on the part of the Sheriff, if not worse" but closed by saying it was satisfied Hutchinson had not connived at the escape, and it offered no comment on the crowd's violence. A week later it quoted the Navasota Tablet's judgment that the sheriff "took no precaution to secure the prisoner."

The Austin Weekly Democratic Statesman ran the brother's interview under the headlines "Murder Most Foul!" and "They Threaten to Hang a Sheriff," describing "Terrible Incitement [Excitement] Among the People" over the killing without criticizing the crowd. It described Washington as the "black corner" of the county because of "a few desperadoes," and said Gee had killed several men before. Neither paper gave the race of anyone involved.

The two accounts differ on how far the crowd went: the Banner's local informant described an assault and a later attempt to capture the sheriff, with no mention of a rope, while the Statesman's interview with the dead man's brother, who sought the sheriff's prosecution, described a near-hanging. They also differ on the crowd's size, 125 to 150 men in the Banner and several hundred in the Statesman.

chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A crowd assaulted the sheriff it blamed for a prisoner's escape [A3]; only the Austin interview says a rope was brought and he was nearly hanged [A4], and no one was killed.

A crowd of 125-150 [A3] or several hundred [A4] acted without authority against a sheriff it accused of conniving at a murder suspect's escape, but no one was killed; at most an attempted lynching, and the near-hanging rests on one second-hand account [A4].
Two independent accounts, a local informant's [A3] and the dead man's brother's [A4], agree that a large crowd turned on Sheriff Hutchinson after Gee escaped, though they differ on how far it went.

The Statesman ran 'They Threaten to Hang a Sheriff' over a reprinted interview, calling the killing 'Murder Most Foul' and the town the 'black corner' of the county because of desperadoes.
